patterns.rhetorical_purpose: Compare 12 frameworks on 9 capability dimensions at a glance.
move_sequence: mark each cell with a checkmark/x/asterisk
patterns.reader_question_answered: Which framework has which capability? (unanswerable from the extracted text)
patterns.signature: an all-visual comparison grid with no cell carrying any text redundancy (no caption sentence stating the pattern the grid shows)
patterns.reader_effect: when the grid is lost (here, to text extraction) or otherwise unavailable, the reader is left with zero information -- there is no prose fallback stating which frameworks have which capabilities
patterns.repair_principle: a comparison table's headline pattern should also be stated once in prose (e.g. 'only OpenHands has all nine'), so the argument survives even if the reader cannot see the table

patterns.section: C RELATED WORK, first paragraph (project/paper.txt line 900-901)
patterns.rhetorical_purpose: Survey many prior multi-agent frameworks quickly.
move_sequence: ... (continues for ~8 frameworks in two long sentences)
patterns.reader_question_answered: What exists already? (but not: why does any of this create a gap for OpenHands specifically?)
patterns.signature: several distinct frameworks introduced in sequence, each described in a short relative clause, with no organizing dimension stated before the list starts
patterns.reader_effect: the reader can follow individual facts but must build the 'gap' argument themselves; the paragraph reads as a survey rather than a case for necessity
patterns.repair_principle: state the organizing dimension (e.g. capability coverage) before naming any individual framework, and end the group with one sentence naming the shared limitation the whole group has -- exactly what section_rules.md's Related-Work contract requires and what this draft's corpus/literature_map.json dimension matrix was built to support
